nodes.label: Aramu and Sarduri I
nodes.full: The Assyrian annals of Shalmaneser III name Arame (Aramu) of Urartu as a king in the mountains around Lake Van in 859–844 BC; a Sarduri, son of Lutipri, then had himself inscribed in Assyrian on the rock of Van Fortress, about 840 BC, as 'king of kings' and builder of its walls. Urartian tradition has these as the first rulers of the kingdom of Biainili (Urartu) and of its capital, Tushpa.
nodes.src: Shalmaneser III annals (RIMA 3); Sarduri I inscription (Van Kalesi); Paul Zimansky, Ancient Ararat (1998); Mirjo Salvini, Geschichte und Kultur der Urartäer (1995).

nodes.label: Ishpuini and Menua
nodes.full: Ishpuini and his son Menua, who ruled jointly for a time, abandoned the Assyrian language for Urartian in their inscriptions and set out an organised kingdom: royal fortresses, a canal to Tushpa, a state cult of Haldi and conquests as far as the Euphrates and Lake Urmia. Menua's inscriptions, more than a hundred, are found over the whole highland.
nodes.src: Salvini 1995; Zimansky 1998; Urartian royal inscriptions (CTU A 3, 5).

nodes.label: Argishti I
nodes.full: Argishti I extended the kingdom north into the Ararat plain, building Erebuni (782 BC, near modern Yerevan) and Argishtihinili (776 BC, Armavir) as provincial centres to settle deportees and hold the fertile plain. His annals, cut in Van Fortress's rock face, list campaigns year by year in the fashion of the Assyrian kings.
nodes.src: Erebuni foundation inscription (CTU A 8-17); Argishti I annals (Horhor chronicle, CTU A 8-1); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Sarduri II
nodes.full: Sarduri II took the kingdom to its greatest extent, with campaigns against the Neo-Hittite states of northern Syria and the Mannaeans and lands in the north, including the first mention of Qulha (Colchis) in a royal text. He built Çavuştepe and other fortresses. He was defeated by Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria in 743 BC, a blow from which Urartu did not recover its dominance in Syria.
nodes.src: Sarduri II inscriptions (CTU A 9); Tiglath-Pileser III annals; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Rusa I
nodes.full: Rusa I tried to rebuild Urartu's position, campaigning around Lake Sevan, intriguing with the Mannaeans and Phrygia against Assyria, and building fortresses near the lake. His reign ended in 714 BC in the disaster of Sargon II's invasion and a defeat by the Cimmerians; Assyrian sources say he took his own life.
nodes.src: Rusa I inscriptions (CTU A 10); Sargon II eighth campaign letter to Ashur; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Argishti II and Rusa II
nodes.full: After the shock of 714 the state, under Argishti II (714–685) and Rusa II (685–645), made peace with Assyria and entered its last prosperous century. Rusa II built great fortress-estates at Teishebaini (Karmir Blur) on the Hrazdan, Ayanis on Lake Van and Bastam in the south, each with temples and warehouses for grain and wine.
nodes.src: Rusa II inscriptions (CTU A 12); Ayanis and Karmir Blur excavation reports; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: The last kings
nodes.full: The names of Sarduri III, Erimena and a Rusa III appear in few inscriptions after the middle of the seventh century, and Assyrian sources go silent as Assyria itself fell. The kingdom ended in the early sixth century, in a way we cannot document: the fortresses were destroyed by fire and later the lands appear under Median and then Persian rule.
nodes.src: Late Urartian inscriptions (CTU A 12-14); Zimansky 1998; Salvini 1995.

nodes.label: Diauehi
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser I of Assyria names Daiaeni, a land and its king Sieni, in the northern highlands in about 1110 BC, and Urartian kings from Menua on record the conquest of 'Diauehi', whose ruler Utupursi gave tribute and gold. Diauehi is the best attested early polity in the north-west of the Caucasus, and many scholars see in it an ancestor of the Georgian lands of Tao.
nodes.src: Tiglath-Pileser I annals (RIMA 2); Menua and Argishti I inscriptions; Salvini 1995; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Qulha
nodes.full: An inscription of Sarduri II records the conquest of 'Qulha', generally taken to be the first appearance of Colchis in a written source. The region of the Rioni valley and the Black Sea plain was ruled by local chieftains with a distinct material culture, and lay at the edge of the known world.
nodes.src: Sarduri II inscription (CTU A 9-1); Lordkipanidze, Archäologie in Georgien (1991); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Colchian kingdom
nodes.full: In the Early Iron Age the Colchian culture reached its flowering, with fortified towns such as Vani, Nokalakevi and Sairkhe, cemeteries of rich burials in the Rioni and Black Sea lowlands and iron and gold working on a large scale. Greek memory, with Aia and King Aeëtes, preserved an image of a rich and powerful kingdom at the end of the sea.
nodes.src: Lordkipanidze 1991; Vani excavation reports (Lordkipanidze et al.); Sagona, The Archaeology of the Caucasus (2018).

nodes.label: Khojaly–Gadabay culture
nodes.full: In the hills and valleys of Karabakh, Gadabay and the Kura basin, a culture of the late second and early first millennium BC has produced rich stone-cist and kurgan tombs with bronze weapons, ornaments and pottery, and settlements with stone walls. The culture's name, from the site of Khojaly in Karabakh and Gadabay in western Azerbaijan, is an archaeological label for a mixed pastoral and farming society.
nodes.src: I. Narimanov and others on Khojaly–Gadabay; Sagona 2018; Kohl, The Making of Bronze Age Eurasia (2007).

nodes.label: Koban culture
nodes.full: In the high valleys of the central Caucasus, the Koban culture of Ossetia and neighbouring districts of Georgia made bronze axes, belts and ornaments of fine workmanship and traded them far to the north and south. It is the best known of the Iron Age mountain cultures, with contacts between the mountain and plain peoples.
nodes.src: E. Chantre, Recherches anthropologiques dans le Caucase (1886–87); Sagona 2018; Kohl 2007.

nodes.label: Shalmaneser III against Urartu
nodes.full: Shalmaneser III of Assyria led his army into the mountain region around Lake Van in 859, 856, 855, 853 and 845 BC, burning fortified towns of Arame's land and claiming victories, but he did not take the capital. The first of his campaigns brought the name Urartu into the written record.
nodes.src: Shalmaneser III annals and Black Obelisk (RIMA 3); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Arpad
nodes.full: In 743 BC Tiglath-Pileser III defeated Sarduri II and a coalition of Syrian rulers in Kummuh, and then besieged Arpad for three years. The campaign broke Urartian influence in northern Syria and Assyria's mastery over the Syrian states opened the road west.
nodes.src: Tiglath-Pileser III annals (Tadmor); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Musasir
nodes.full: In 714 BC Sargon II marched through Mannea, defeated Rusa I's army, and turned south-west to the holy city of Musasir, where he plundered the temple of Haldi and carried away its god and treasure. The detailed account of this campaign, a 430-line letter to the god Ashur, is the fullest document for Urartu in any language.
nodes.src: Sargon II, Letter to the god Ashur (TCL 3); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Cimmerians
nodes.full: Nomads called Gimirru in Assyrian texts (Cimmerians) arrived from the steppe north of the Caucasus in the late eighth century and defeated Rusa I's army, according to Sargon's agents; they then rode across Anatolia into Phrygia and Lydia. Their origin and their material culture are uncertain, and they are known mainly from enemy texts.
nodes.src: Sargon II's letters (SAA 5); Esarhaddon prisms; Ivantchik, Les Cimmériens au Proche-Orient (1993).

nodes.label: Scythians
nodes.full: Another steppe people, the Scythians (Ishkuzai), appear in the seventh century as raiders and mercenaries in the lands between Urartu, Mannea and Assyria; their king Ishpakaia appears in Esarhaddon's records about 679 BC and Bartatua later married an Assyrian princess. Greek sources placed them in control of Media for decades, a claim which is debated.
nodes.src: Esarhaddon inscriptions (RINAP 4); Herodotus 1.103–106; Ivantchik 1993.

nodes.label: Burning of Teishebaini
nodes.full: The fortress-city of Teishebaini on Karmir Blur ('red hill') was destroyed by fire, with its stores of grain and wine, its bronze objects and arms left in the ruins; Armenian and Russian excavations from 1939 to 1971 found arrowheads and charred roofs. By whom, and when, is unknown: Medes, Scythians, Cimmerians and a local rising have all been proposed.
nodes.src: Boris Piotrovsky, Karmir-Blur (1950, 1952); Piotrovsky, The Ancient Civilization of Urartu (1969); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Menua’s and Argishti’s wars
nodes.full: Menua and Argishti I's rock-cut annals list year by year the lands subdued, among them Etiuni, Diauehi, Mannea and the Hittite lands on the Euphrates, with the counts of captives and animals taken. The wars made Urartu the principal rival of Assyria.
nodes.src: Menua inscriptions; Argishti I annals (Horhor chronicle); Salvini 1995.

nodes.label: Kingdom of fortresses
nodes.full: The Urartian state was ruled from fortress-towns in a network of over 100 sites, each with its governor, garrison and storehouses, joined by roads and by messengers, and tied to the king by tax in kind and conscription. The king was the highest ruler of the 'country of Biainili', and the state cult of Haldi gave the whole its ideology.
nodes.src: Zimansky 1998; Salvini 1995; Piotrovsky 1969.

nodes.label: Inscriptions and tablets
nodes.full: More than 500 Urartian inscriptions, cut in rock, on stelae, bronze and clay, record building, victories and offerings; a few dozen clay tablets from Teishebaini and Bastam record supplies and storage. The language is Urartian, related to Hurrian, and the script is Assyrian cuneiform adapted for it.
nodes.src: Corpus dei testi urartei (CTU), ed. Salvini (2008); Salvini 1995.

nodes.label: Deportation
nodes.full: Menua, Argishti I and their successors moved tens of thousands of captives from conquered lands, often artisans and farmers, to the royal fortresses and new foundations of the north, as the inscriptions state with figures: Argishti claims some 6,600 persons settled at Erebuni. It was a means of populating Argishtihinili and the plain.
nodes.src: Erebuni foundation inscription (CTU A 8-17); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Vassals
nodes.full: Beyond the core, kings of Diauehi, Colchis and the Mannaean marches acknowledged Urartu by tribute and troops, while keeping their own rulers, a pattern similar to the Assyrian client system. The distance of Colchis and the Kura lands from Tushpa made the control weak.
nodes.src: Salvini 1995; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Haldi, Teisheba, Shivini
nodes.full: A rock inscription at Meher Kapısı near Van, set up by Ishpuini and Menua about 810 BC, lists the offerings due to some 79 gods at 'the door of Haldi', headed by Haldi, the warlike god of Urartu's kings, Teisheba the storm god and Shivini the sun god. It is the best statement of the state religion.
nodes.src: Meher Kapısı inscription (CTU A 3-1); Salvini 1995; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Musasir temple
nodes.full: The sanctuary of Haldi at Ardini or Musasir, on the south-eastern border of the kingdom, was an old religious centre, perhaps where Urartian kings were crowned; its plunder by Sargon II in 714 BC is described in detail, with a list of the gold, silver and bronze removed from it, and the god himself was led into captivity.
nodes.src: Sargon II, Letter to Ashur; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Rock niches and susi temples
nodes.full: Urartian cult places were of two kinds, rock-cut niches with steps and inscriptions, such as the Haldi Gate at Meher Kapısı, and the 'susi' temple, a tower-like square building with thick walls. Rusa II's temple at Ayanis, from about 672 BC, with its foundation text and offering lists, is the best preserved.
nodes.src: Altan Çilingiroğlu, Ayanis excavations; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Urartian bronzes
nodes.full: Urartian metalworkers made cauldrons on tripods with bulls' heads and siren attachments, belts and quivers with scenes of hunting and battle, helmets and shields with lion friezes bearing the names of kings. Examples were taken as booty to Assyria and exported to Greece, Phrygia and Etruria.
nodes.src: Piotrovsky 1969; Seton Lloyd, Early Highland Peoples of Anatolia (1967); Kellner on Urartian metalwork.

nodes.label: Frescoes of Erebuni
nodes.full: In the royal halls of the fortress of Erebuni, the walls were covered with painted friezes of deities, lions, bulls, rosettes and processions on a ground of red and blue. Excavated from 1950 by Konstantin Hovhannisyan and Arkady Martirosyan, they were partly restored, and the site is the museum of Yerevan's foundation.
nodes.src: K. Hovhannisyan, Erebuni excavation reports (1950–); A. Martirosyan, Argishtikhinili (1974).

nodes.label: Rock-cut tombs
nodes.full: On the cliff of Van Fortress, the 'Horhor' tomb cut into the rock and the royal tomb chambers of Argishti I, with long inscriptions, are the best-known rock-cut monuments of Urartu; the Persian king Xerxes later added his own trilingual inscription on the cliff beside them.
nodes.src: Zimansky 1998; Xerxes inscription XV (Van).

nodes.label: Colchian gold
nodes.full: Colchian burials contain gold diadems, ornaments of filigree and granulation, bronze figures of animals, and weapons, a craft tradition with connections to the Near East and, later, to the Greek world. The most spectacular finds come from Vani and Sairkhe.
nodes.src: Lordkipanidze 1991; Vani excavation reports.

nodes.label: Urartian language
nodes.full: The Urartian language, known only from the royal inscriptions and a few documents, is related to Hurrian, and the two form a separate family, the Hurro-Urartian, with no known living relatives. It is not Indo-European, and no direct ancestry to Armenian is claimed; the script was borrowed from Assyria.
nodes.src: Gernot Wilhelm, 'Urartian' in R. Woodard (ed.), The Ancient Languages of Asia Minor (2008); Salvini 1995.

nodes.label: Herodotus’s Colchians
nodes.full: Herodotus, who had not visited Colchis, wrote that the Colchians were descended from a part of the army of the Egyptian king Sesostris, left behind at the Phasis, because they had dark skin and woolly hair and practised circumcision and linen-working like the Egyptians. The account is part of Greek speculation on origins, and not an independent record.
nodes.src: Herodotus 2.104–105.

nodes.label: Argonauts
nodes.full: The Greek epic of Jason and the Argonauts, who sailed to the land of King Aeëtes at the Phasis to take the golden fleece, is already known to Homer and Hesiod, and its geography ties the end of the Black Sea to an image of untold wealth. Strabo explained the fleece by the Colchian practice of catching gold dust in sheepskins in the rivers.
nodes.src: Homer, Odyssey 12.69–72; Hesiod, Theogony 956–962; Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica; Strabo 11.2.19.

nodes.label: Ararat
nodes.full: In the Hebrew Bible, the ark of Noah comes to rest 'upon the mountains of Ararat' (Genesis 8:4), and the sons of Sennacherib flee 'into the land of Ararat' after killing their father (2 Kings 19:37), using the Hebrew form of Urartu. The name thus passed into the tradition as the region and, later, the mountain itself.
nodes.src: Genesis 8:4; 2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38; Jeremiah 51:27.

nodes.label: Canals, grain, wine
nodes.full: Royal canals, gardens and vineyards, described in inscriptions, supported a farming economy of barley, wheat and grapes on irrigated land. The storerooms of Karmir Blur held rows of buried pithoi that contained wine and grain, with labels in cuneiform and Urartian hieroglyphic signs, and the wine cellars of Teishebaini contain scores of vats.
nodes.src: Piotrovsky 1969; Zimansky 1998; Menua canal inscription.

nodes.label: Metals, horses, herds
nodes.full: Urartu's wealth rested on the ores of the highlands, copper and iron, which its smiths turned into weapons, bronze vessels and tools, and on herds, particularly horses, which Assyrian kings counted among their booty. The state drew on these through tribute and its workshops.
nodes.src: Zimansky 1998; Piotrovsky 1969; Assyrian annals on booty.

nodes.label: Gold and iron of Colchis
nodes.full: Colchis was known to the Greeks for gold, which Strabo says was washed in the rivers with fleeces, and for iron, flax and timber. The finds at Vani and Sairkhe, and iron production sites in the Rioni valley, confirm a gold and metalworking economy of regional importance.
nodes.src: Strabo 11.2.19; Lordkipanidze 1991; Sagona 2018.

nodes.label: Menua canal
nodes.full: Menua had a canal of some 50 kilometres cut from the Hoşap valley to bring water to the plain of Tushpa, passing over rock and across valleys on stone embankments. An inscription states his name and the canal's purpose. It is known locally as the Shamiram canal, and parts of it have remained in use down to modern times.
nodes.src: Menua canal inscription (CTU A 5-11); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Cyclopean fortresses
nodes.full: Urartian engineers cut and fitted massive stones, without mortar, into walls with salients, terraces and rock-cut cisterns, placing their citadels on crags and spurs; Çavuştepe, Ayanis, Bastam and Erebuni are the best-preserved. The method was a model for later highland fortification.
nodes.src: Zimansky 1998; Çilingiroğlu on Ayanis.

nodes.label: Iron
nodes.full: Iron objects appear in the highlands and the Caucasus from the end of the second millennium, at first as ornaments and weapons, and by the eighth and seventh centuries as tools and arms in quantity. Iron-working in Colchis and in the Armenian highlands has been regarded as one of the early centres, but the question of whether it was the source or a recipient is open.
nodes.src: Sagona 2018; Kohl 2007; Chernykh, Ancient Metallurgy in the USSR (1992).

nodes.label: Bronzes in Greek sanctuaries
nodes.full: Cauldron attachments in the form of bulls' heads and sirens, of Urartian make or of imitations, were deposited as votive offerings in the sanctuaries of Olympia, Samos, Delphi and in Etruscan tombs, and were a model for Greek bronze-workers. They are the best material evidence of Urartian contacts with the Aegean.
nodes.src: Seton Lloyd 1967; Kyrieleis on bronzes at Samos; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Midas and Rusa
nodes.full: Assyrian letters report that Mita of Mushki, the Midas of the Phrygians, and Rusa of Urartu made contact in the years before 710, and that Midas then made peace with Sargon, perhaps because of the Cimmerian threat to both. The records show a diplomatic web from the Aegean to the highlands.
nodes.src: Sargon II's annals and letters (SAA 1, 5); Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Greek colonies
nodes.full: Milesian Greeks founded trading settlements at Phasis (Poti), at the mouth of the Rioni, and at Dioscurias (Sukhumi) in the late seventh or sixth century BC, to trade in metal, timber, flax and slaves, and they became channels for Greek goods into the interior of Colchis. The date of the foundations is debated.
nodes.src: Pseudo-Scylax, Periplus; Strabo 11.2.17; Pichvnari excavation reports (Kacharava, Kvirkvelia).

nodes.label: Media and the end of Assyria
nodes.full: The capture of Nineveh in 612 BC by the Babylonians and Medes ended the Assyrian empire which had been Urartu's main rival; within a few decades Urartu too had gone and the highland region fell to the Median state, which by about 585 BC had reached the Halys river in Anatolia. The power vacuum was filled from the east.
nodes.src: Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 3); Herodotus 1.73–74; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: Steppe peoples
nodes.full: The Cimmerians and Scythians who struck at Urartu and Assyria were part of a general movement of mounted peoples from the Pontic steppe, a change linked to the spread of iron and of mounted warfare. Their routes passed on both sides of the Caucasus range.
nodes.src: Ivantchik 1993; Kohl 2007.

nodes.label: Workers of the archive
nodes.full: Clay tablets from Teishebaini list deliveries of grain and wine, and rations for dependants of the fortress, among whom workers and slaves are named. Their names are Urartian, Hurrian and others, and show a mixed population of the fortress estate.
nodes.src: Karmir Blur tablets (CTU B); Piotrovsky 1969.

nodes.label: Deportees
nodes.full: Prisoners from conquered lands, including Hittite and Mannaean farmers, were settled on the royal estates in the Ararat plain and Van as labourers and craftsmen, as the inscriptions of Argishti I and Sarduri II state, and their numbers run to thousands. Their own words survive nowhere.
nodes.src: Erebuni foundation inscription; Argishti I annals; Zimansky 1998.

nodes.label: A queen
nodes.full: Few women are named in Urartian texts. Queen Tariria, wife of Menua, appears in a dedicatory text and has a stele with her own name, showing that a royal woman could found a building and hold property in her own right.
nodes.src: Tariria inscription (CTU A 5-22); Salvini 1995.

nodes.label: Uruatri and the Nairi lands
nodes.full: Shalmaneser I of Assyria (1274–1245 BC) records a campaign against the land of Uruatri, a group of eight mountain lands, the earliest mention of the name later given as Urartu.
nodes.src: background — see the Kura–Araxes and the Bronze Age Caucasus folio (caucasus-3500bc-1200bc)
